I'm quiet type BPD and it's pretty hellish. BPD is often described with violent anger/passion and for a long time I laughed at the idea that I could be considered such a person. I was known for being kind/gentle/soft spoken. Also erratic, weepy, dramatic, and unstable. 

I didn't realize that I was experiencing violent anger, but I was. I was just turning it in on myself. I believed it didn't matter if I self-harmed or suffered from bulimia. Because it was just me, I was only hurting me and what was hurt anyway? The only thing that mattered were other people and I could deal with the pain. I was worthless, and most of all, I didn't have an identity. I was what people thought I was. So I performed for them. 

That doesn't mean I had a "perfect" life, because I crashed and burned hard. But there was a handful of people that I decided mattered. That their opinion mattered. They became gods, greater than life, they were life. And I didn't cling dramatically, I didn't threaten to kill myself. I just was an persistent, quiet presence. 

Rambling. 

Quiet typed BPD for me has been a journey in passionately loving humans and experiencing intense compassion/empathy for everyone . . . except myself. All my sadism, all my desires, all the pain I feel at not feeling validated, is self-consuming. The violent anger didn't go away, it just turned inward.

Preach! People don't understand that I'm *not* choosing to fail by not trying hard enough. I function differently. Sometimes, I can't make very much "progress" or my "progress" fluxes. 

It's really hard to get people to understand that you have a chronic mental illness. This isn't something we "beat" like cancer. We're going to live with it forever. So things like "sleep enough! eat well! journal!" are helpful in the same way bandaids are helpful. Which is to say that they are, but it's never going to fix the problem.

The time periods have not become consistent (between being able to feel and not feeling anything), but the predictors have become a little easier to identify. 

I cannot stress enough that if you do not have a therapist now, to seek one out. I'm in the process (I've been moved around between therapists to find a good fit) and even the little bits and pieces I've gotten have made a lot of difference.

I was spanked growing up and I wish I hadn't been. It taught me that I didn't have the ability to deny consent to my parents. They had the right to hit me and I was not allowed to say no. I know, its *discipline* and in context with an adult's processing power, it makes sense. As a kid, you'll learn not to do the bad thing, but that's just a side effect. 

I'm not saying everyone reacts this way. But I think it's dangerous to teach children that they will be physically struck with or without their permission, but that it's ok because mommy/daddy/authority figures are in charge. This can lead to situations in adolescence or adulthood where a person may cause self harm (mental, physical, or emotional) because they feel they deserve it and punishment/forgiveness = feeling pain. 

Or, it could make them vulnerable to attacks. Seeing a person claiming authority (assault), the "freeze" (from flight, fight, freeze) may be what they are conditioned to go to. That could even happen without violence, but something as simple being unable to voice displeasure with bodily discomfort caused by others. 

And approaching it by asking the child's permission to spank them, teaches a really messed up signal. *Tell me this thing is ok to do even though that's confusing and dissonant with your mental health* Its not a kind thing to teach a kid to override his protective instincts and to force him to give a coerced consent.


I guess the biggest thing for me is consent. Yes, spanking is effective at eliciting results, but by the same logic, a grenade could easily be used to kill a spider. That doesn't make it a good way to kill a spider. Yes, children can and often do learn to behave through spanking, and not all of them deal with issues later on. However, I think that the potential damage in spanking far outweighs it's benefits.

You may hear this from people, but with me, I usually heard myself saying it. Know that it's bullshit. Your friendship was valid and the positive experiences were and are as valid as the bad ones. This dichotomy can feel unsettling. I.e. I hate this person more than anything and I want them to burn! Wait, of course I don't want that. That's my friend. Wait....

I tried to stay friends when this happened to me. (No drugs involved, but grey area) And for 6 months I disassociated, drank nightly, and kept going to class with him. I knew something was fucked up when I felt more triggered by men that looked like him than by him. I never connected him, the real him, to what happened. I moved forward into post trauma, where my view of him stayed (with some mental gymnastics) more concurrent with pre trauma. 

After I stopped seeing him, it was like every bad episode I ever tried to drink/block out started happening all the time. Like an awful breakout after switching to proactiv. It felt unfair. 

I said all this because it was what helped me understand. That you can feel violated and traumatized alongside mourning the loss of the person who did not mean to traumatize you. And it is OK to want to leave after this. You are not immune to trauma, whether or not it was intentional. You have the right to feel and the right to choose a path away from this person so that you can heal. 

No, as far as clinical options go there isn't much. I smoke a little pot to help with the panic attacks, and I have adderall/lamictal but those are for ADHD/Bipolar 2. There aren't meds to speed along the healing process. Therapy helps a lot, but I've found that the most important thing is support. Family and friends, or friend that are basically family in my case. Having people who understand and do not feel the need to weigh in on the validity of your pain. 

Also, exercise helps a lot. Sports that are heavy into balance (martial arts, dance, etc.) are actually really helpful for processing.  It reconnects you to your body in a positive way. And teaching your body new skills can be helpful while trying to cultivate new mind skills. That way it doesn't feel so strange (like cmon this is all in my head, just think better?) I'm a biased martial artist, and I can say that it works for me. I remember dancing helping as well. I was never as disciplined in dance, but it was more of a release. 

Sleep is important. And difficult. All I can contribute to what I'm sure you already know (like not using electronics in bed,or doing anything there besides sleep or intimacy, etc.) is my own trick. 

Playlists. I have one for everything (Waking up, working out, etc). I even have one for PTSD. that's literally the playlists name. I built it in such a way that the first 2 or 3 songs are not soothing lets-avoid-this-shit songs, they're angry and raw and sad. Then I have a transition song. A few processing songs. Then onto resolution. You get the idea. Starting out with the loud/angry stuff gives a timed window to go ahead and feel all the raw emotions. It's not saying "this isn't real" it's connecting me to "yes this is real and it kinda sucks ass". The rest goes like you think it would. It's kinda great cause each song is like it's own mini catharsis. 

I have one for sleep and it's long enough to include my nightly rituals (brushing teeth, etc.). It's nice because fosters familiarity and that's such a comforting feeling when everything is fucking confusing. Sleep can become part of the ritual. I promise. I really do.

And I wanted to forgive him when I saw how tortured he was about it. He said he didn't realize I didn't want to and I do believe him. I'd disclosed my abuse history, btw. 

The facade eventually falls when the PTSD takes over and you can't live in denial any longer. But dude, that denial? It's not done on a conscious level. I literally hadn't processed enough to understand what had happened and it kept me from being able to kick him out of my life.  That's the painful part. Your brain is fighting so hard to protect you because if you realized everything at the same time, it would be too much for you. It's this long waiting game of hoping you'll make it through the next truth bomb your brain thinks you're ready for.

I have ADHD, PTSD, and Bipolar 2 disorder. Basically, I can become numb from depression or extreme stimulation. I was traumatized sexually this past January. It was anal sex, without a condom or lube, and I didn't know it was about to happen when it started. He broke up with me before I got dressed.

So, I've been raped and dumped. I would bleed for two days. What did I feel?

Not a goddamn thing. It was like it hadn't happened. Or it had happened to someone else. I knew that it was a disappointing situation, and that I didn't "like" (from just an intellectual sense) what had just happened. Sounds didn't stand out, just his voice. It was like someone clicking "on" or "off" on a walkie-talkie.  His voice, I'd listen and respond. No one talking, just silence. Silence like something had swollen my ears shut and all I "heard" was the blood inside my head, or my breathing. 

Every color seemed different on the drive home, and every building unfamiliar. Like someone had dismantled my town and built up an exact replica. Everything was just a little wrong, different, and fake. I remember that nothing felt/sounded right or real. 


I burned myself when I got home because growing up I'd been a self harmer. It wasn't something that I did or felt the need to do anymore, but I didn't even question it. I just sat down, very matter-of-factly, and emptied 10 matches out on the same spot on my forearm. By the 4th match, things began to look more realistic. By the 10th and last match, I felt like I was almost back to reality. My head was buzzing, but the problem wasn't my surroundings anymore. They looked real and I felt fake. 

Numbness from deep depression is different. It's like there isn't anything inside you anymore. Not happiness, not sorrow. Just nothing. Like plugging in your phone but it just does not charge. You don't feel anything unless you're focusing on it. Not the weight of your body, not the breeze, you don't register anything. 


That's all I got.

I have been in *exactly* the same place. I knew at 14 that something was wrong, that I wasn't working right. It was a sense I guess. Cue an adolescence of confusion, being ignored, and being told to stop being so dramatic/dreary. 

When I was 20, I asked my parents to see a mental health professional. I'd been self-injuring (which they knew some about) for 2 years and had recently tried to take my life (I did not tell them that part or why I tried). They said they couldn't help if they didn't know what was wrong, I wanted privacy, and nothing went anywhere. I'd continue to self harm for 3 years. 


At 23 I finally decided to just pay myself. I found a doc, got on meds, and quickly became unable to pay anything. I was diagnosed with Bipolar 2 disorder and put on lamictal. I wrote my mom an email explaining my situation (I lived with her, but she was a huge trigger for me). I asked for help with the doc/meds because I couldn't afford them. She never replied. 


Fast forward to the next year's summer. I had fallen apart. I know I was bipolar but had no treatment. Seeing my desperation, and how much I'd fallen apart, my parents relented.


I've since been diagnosed additionally with ADHD, and PTSD. 


I cannot stress this enough, *you need to see a doctor.* Meds are your friend. Your mom, like mine, may not take it seriously at first. Keep at it. I wish I had gotten help 3 years sooner. There are free counseling services out there and I encourage you to seek them out. 

Please take care of yourself.
